_comment: Role materials for the Creative Negotiations sales-job scenario. Edit this file (and the scenario it links to) to change what participants see and how offers are scored; the app reloads it at every game start, no redeploy needed. `roles` follows the Empirica loader's format (one role per file). `scenario_url` points at the scorer's scenario JSON (issues, ranges, payoffs for both roles) used by server/src/score_offer/score_offer.py. `scorer_role` is the role name inside that scenario.

roles.narrative:
**CANDIDATE** **ROLE INFORMATION** You are an ambitious sales professional negotiating a role with a young company. You care about income, but money isn't all that matters in life. You want room to build a career, protect time with your family, and avoid getting stuck in a role where your work is visible but you are not developing professionally. Your objective is to reach an agreement with the highest total score you can, while recognizing that the Recruiter has priorities of their own that may conflict with yours. Every complete offer must include three terms: **salary**, a **starting date**, and a **personal budget for work expenses** such as client travel, meals, and lodging (but not take-home pay!). You prefer a higher salary and budget and an earlier start. • Annual salary may range from $20,000 to $80,000: $20,000 gives you −2 points,
$40,000 gives you 0, and $80,000 gives you +2. • Starting dates may range from 1 May to 30 September: 1 May gives you +2,
around 16 July gives you 0, and 30 September gives you −2. • The personal budget may range from $1,000 to $20,000: $1,000 gives you −2,
$10,500 gives you 0, and $20,000 gives you +2. The platform calculates intermediate scores automatically. For example, a $7,000 budget is worth about −0.74 points to you. You do not need to calculate this yourself. These headline contract terms are easy to put numbers on. However, the interview also left you thinking about what the job would actually be like and what other terms you might ask for given what matters to you. **Background Information** On the way home, you think about the company's usual 30 vacation days per year and 3 remote-working days per week. Those arrangements seem reasonable. Each is worth 0 points to you. Still, more flexibility would mean more time with your family and more room for interests and professional development outside work, while less flexibility would work against those interests. • For vacation, 10 days per year are worth −1 point to you and 50 days are worth +1. • For remote work, 1 day per week is worth −1 and all 5 working days are worth +1. The two terms are scored separately, with proportional points for values in between. You also remember the Recruiter's stories about how people grow in the company. • One new hire attended an external professional training program; another was paired with an experienced mentor. • Someone else built relationships with senior colleagues after volunteering at a recruitment fair. Those examples appealed to you because they offered concrete ways to learn and build relationships rather than vague promises of “growth.” Other stories were less appealing. • The Recruiter joked that sociable employees often end up organizing team events. • Good client stories are turned into LinkedIn posts, and confident employees sometimes present at conferences. … You enjoy people, but you do not want every spare hour turned into company visibility. A recruitment fair might expand your network; recurring publicity work might simply expand your workload. That evening, your spouse asked whether the company would support the professional association that has helped you and what would happen if you eventually wanted to leave. • Sponsored membership could help keep your skills and outside relationships alive. • The question about leaving brought you back to the non-compete clause you had raised. • You want to show commitment without unnecessarily limiting your future. The interview contained small details and examples rather than a neat menu of contract features. Some may simply be background. Others could become useful terms if you connect them to what matters to you. **Your Task** Negotiate with the Recruiter by making offers in plain, ordinary language, as if you were writing them a short message. Every complete offer must include salary, a personal work-expense budget, and a starting date. You decide what else is worth discussing and when to raise it. **For example:** “I propose a salary of [amount], a personal work-expense budget of [amount], and a starting date of [date], together with [list any job features you want to bring up].” Use your own values and wording. **Your score** is private and **translates** directly into the **bonus payment you** can **earn** from this task. • You may propose an offer worth zero or less to you, but you can accept only an offer worth more than zero to you. • An agreement requires both parties to accept the same offer, with a positive total score for you and the Recruiter. **Important notes on offers and scoring** 1. Without a deal, you will continue your job search; you do not have another offer in hand. This fallback is worth 0 points. 2. The researchers set the scoring rules in advance, and the platform calculates points automatically; you do not assign or calculate points yourself. 3. Each additional contract feature introduced in the negotiation is worth **between** −1 and +1 points to you, based on the interests in your role. Its value to the Recruiter may differ. 4. **You are not limited to the job features described or suggested here. You may creatively introduce other plausible contract features or job arrangements.** 5. Some features you introduce may not fit the situation and will be worth 0 points. But that doesn't mean you should hold back on creative and thoughtful ideas!
roles.BATNA: If you do not reach an agreement, you receive 0 points. An agreement only counts if the total score is above zero for both parties.

tips:
Negotiation is a skill you can get better at with practice. At its core, it is about making choices when people want different things, with each person’s decision affecting what the others get out of the deal. The good news is that a few basic ideas go a long way.

One of the most important ideas is knowing your best alternative to negotiating an agreement, or your BATNA. This is your realistic fallback plan outside the negotiation. Knowing what that alternative is actually worth helps protect you from accepting an agreement that leaves you worse off than walking away. A simple rule follows from this: never accept a deal worse than your BATNA.

Another key idea is that some negotiations can be win-win. This happens when people value different issues differently. If something matters a lot to you but not as much to the other person, you may be able to trade it for something you care about more. In practice, this means focusing less on “splitting the difference” and more on learning what the other person really wants, so you can make smart tradeoffs that leave both of you better off.

A final tip is that win-win outcomes become easier to achieve when everyone knows what matters most to each party . So try to be clear about what you care about, and how these interests translate to what you want across each issue under negotiation. At the same time, listen closely to what the other person cares about. Knowing this is what will make such smart, win-win tradeoffs possible.
